concept.shortExplanation: One attention pattern per layer would force every relationship a sentence contains through a single set of weights. Instead the layer splits its dimensions into several heads, each with its own query, key and value projections, each computing an independent pattern, and concatenates the results. Nothing assigns roles to heads — but train the model and heads reliably specialise anyway, some tracking position, some syntax, some parking on delimiters. You are about to extract all of them from a real model and measure what each one does.
concept.ahaMoment: Head specialisation was never designed. It is what happens when you give a model several parallel channels and a loss that rewards using them for different things.

modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The transformer could not be downloaded, so per-head attention cannot be extracted. Check your connection and retry — cached models work offline.

levels.title: Spot the Specialist
levels.instructions: All twelve heads of this layer, side by side, computed live. Find the head that attends almost entirely to the previous token — its behaviour is measured directly from its real attention matrix.

engineConfig.sentence: the quiet librarian returned the overdue book yesterday morning

hints: Look at layer 0 first. Earlier layers are where raw positional patterns like "attend to the previous token" tend to show up most cleanly, before later layers drift toward delimiter-heavy attention.
A previous-token head's matrix has weight concentrated one cell to the left of the diagonal in almost every row. Scan the twelve mini-matrices for that stripe rather than reading the numbers.

At layer 0, head 2 attends to the immediately preceding token with about 0.83 average weight, and it's the only head at that layer classified previous-token — every other head is diffuse. Nominate head 2 in all three rounds for a perfect score.

levels.title: Classify Every Head
levels.instructions: Assign a behaviour label to each head in the layer. Ground truth comes from statistics computed over each head's real attention matrix — offset concentration, entropy and delimiter mass.

engineConfig.sentence: after the meeting ended, the team walked to the cafe across the street

hints: Not every head has a clean label. Heads whose top two behaviour scores are close together are excluded from grading entirely — this level's margin is 0.12, so spend your effort on the heads with an unambiguous pattern rather than guessing on borderline ones.
A delimiter head lights up a whole column at [CLS] or [SEP] no matter which row (query) you look at. A diffuse head has no strong single pattern — weight spread out fairly evenly across the row.

At layer 2, 7 of the 12 heads are gradable: heads 0, 4, 7, 9 and 11 are delimiter specialists; heads 6 and 10 are diffuse. Heads 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 fall below the confidence margin and aren't graded either way. Labelling those 7 correctly scores a perfect 1.0.

levels.title: Which Head Solves It?
levels.instructions: Your own sentence, containing a long-range dependency. Find the single head anywhere in the model that most strongly links the two tokens you care about, and see how localised that capability really is.

engineConfig.sentence: the keys that the neighbour returned last week are still on the table

hints: The default sentence hides a subject-verb pair split by a relative clause: "the keys that the neighbour returned last week are still on the table." The verb "are" has to agree with "keys", many tokens earlier — that split is the long-range dependency to hunt for.

Attention isn't symmetric — the direction you probe matters, and the answer isn't always in the layer you start on. Probe from the later token back to the earlier one, and move the layer slider since the search spans every layer, not just the one shown.
Probing from "are" (token 9) back to "keys" (token 2) at layer 3, head 1 finds a weight of 0.896 — the strongest link for that pair anywhere in the model, so it scores a perfect 1.0.
